title: Visualizing murine breast and melanoma tumor microenvironment using intravital multiphoton microscopy
protocol: Assess the tumor-bearing mouse for any visible signs of distress.
Anesthetize the mouse according to its body weight.
Administer injectable anesthesia, ketamine/xylazine (100/10 mg/kg) combined dose to provide deep surgical-plane anesthesia.
Carefully remove the abdominal hair using an electric shaver.
Remove 80%–90% of hair by shaving until very little hair remains around the poorly accessible regions such as the hindlimbs.
Take care to avoid damaging the skin overlying the tumor when using an electric shaver.
Apply a depilatory cream such as Nair or Veet to the whole abdomen after shaving.
Clean the hair removal cream with a wet tissue after 1-2 minutes.
Thoroughly clean and tap-dry the skin with dry tissues.
Swab the area with moist, lint-free paper.
Place the mouse on its back on a thermal heating pad to maintain core body temperature.
Move the needle of an insulin syringe side-to-side using an artery/toothed-forceps until it breaks from the syringe.
Insert the broken/blunt end of the needle into PE10 tubing to create a cannula.
Insert a needle connected to a 3-way stopcock on the other end of the PE10 tubing for administering drugs, dyes, or cells.
Anesthetize the mouse.
Disinfect the tail by swabbing with 70% w/v ethanol.
Warm the tail under a heat lamp for 1–2 minutes.
Observe the lateral veins within the tail.
Once the blood vessel appears dilated, proceed with cannulation.
Lift the tail firmly.
Position the needle of the cannula on top of the distal end of the tail parallel to the vessel.
Tilt the needle to an angle of 10°–15° and insert the bevel into the blood vessel.
Draw the syringe attached to the cannula to check if blood enters the tubing.
If blood does not enter, repeat the process carefully in another region of the tail.
Hold the needle attached to the cannula with artery/toothed forceps using the dominant hand.
Immobilize the needle and tubing on the tail using surgical tape.
Flush 50–100 μL of saline to prevent blood coagulation within the needle.
Inject drugs and cells via the cannula using a 3-way stopcock if required.
Ensure no more than 10% of the blood volume (approximately 100 μL) is injected at any given time.
Remove hair from approximately 1–2 cm region of skin on the ventral side of the neck using depilatory creams.
Make a superficial skin incision (approximately 1 cm) using fine-tipped surgical scissors right of the midline of the neck (left to the trachea).
Gently tease the skin apart to highlight the underlying tissue.
Using fine forceps, gently tease the underlying fascia and the surrounding tissue whilst avoiding injury.
Immobilize the skin tissue using a surgical suture.
Tape the other end of the suture onto the heating pad or the metal base plate of the imaging stage.
Gently tease the tissue between the common carotid artery, vagus nerve, and jugular vein.
Separate the jugular vein and the vagus nerve from the underlying tissue using ultrafine forceps.
Lift the jugular vein gently with forceps without displacing any underlying tissue.
Separate the vagus nerve and the carotid artery carefully to avoid nerve damage during ligation.
Ligate the anterior region of the jugular vein using an instrument tie methodology with two opposing throws.
Use a surgical silk suture (Dynek Dysilk 4/0) for the ligature.
Clamp the distal end using a microvascular clamp attached to the S&T clamp applying forceps.
Leave a single suture untied at the distal end.
Cut appropriately sized sutures and pass under the vein which has been gently lifted by inserting forceps underneath.
Make a small incision on the vein with Vannas scissors.
Insert a cannula connected to a 3-way stopcock containing saline into the vein via the incision.
Immobilize the cannula in the vein by ligating with a surgical suture employing instrument tie methodology with two opposing throws.
Use a second suture at the distal end of the blood vessel to stabilize the cannula further.
Cut the tip of the cannula with a scalpel blade to provide a sharp 45° bevel.
Confirm that the cannula or connecting stopcock has no air entrapped and the stopcock is in a locked position.
Remove the microvascular clamp using S&T clamp forceps.
Trim excess suture thread.
Place the skin flap on the underlying tissue, seal the incision site using surgical glue.
Attach the cannula onto the skin surface using surgical glue followed by an adhesive bandage if needed.
Flush 50–100 μL of saline through the cannula to prevent blood coagulation.
Inject drugs and cells via the cannula using a 3-way stopcock, ensuring no more than 10% of the blood volume is injected at any given time.
Use ultrafine forceps to separate the common carotid artery from the vagus nerve.
Isolate the carotid artery from underlying tissue.
Gently lift the carotid artery using the forceps.
Ligate the anterior region of the common carotid artery prior to its division into internal and external branches.
Cut appropriately sized sutures (approximately 10 cm in length).
Pass the suture under the lifted artery.
Use silk surgical suture (Dynek Dysilk 4/0) for ligation.
Apply two opposing throws to secure the ligature.
Attach microvascular clamps to S&T clamp using forceps.
Clamp the distal end of the carotid artery.
Using Vannas scissors, make a small incision in the carotid artery.
Lift the artery from the top using Dumont #7 forceps.
Position the Vannas scissors at 45° to the forceps so that just a small part of the artery comes in contact with the scissors.
Make a single, sharp cut to avoid excessive damage to the artery.
Insert a cannula connected to a 3-way stopcock containing saline into the artery via the incision.
Immobilize the cannula in the artery by ligation with a surgical suture.
Use a second suture at the distal end of the blood vessel to stabilize the cannula further if required.
Pull the cannula tube at the tip to make it thin without generating kinks.
Cut the tip of the cannula with a scalpel blade to provide a sharp 30° to 45° bevel.
Confirm that the cannula or connecting stopcock has no air entrapped and the stopcock is in a locked position.
Remove the microvascular clamp using S&T clamp forceps.
Trim excess suture thread.
Place the skin flap on the underlying tissue.
Seal the incision site using surgical glue.
Attach the cannula onto the skin surface using surgical glue followed by an adhesive bandage if necessary.
Flush 50–100 μL of saline to prevent blood coagulation within the cannula.
Inject drugs and cells via the cannula using a 3-way stopcock, ensuring no more than 10% of the blood volume is injected at any given time.
Tape the syringe, 3-way stopcock, and tubing to the stage or heat pad securely.
Pause briefly (<30 sec) between steps 18–24 to prepare for the upcoming step.
Pause briefly (<30 sec) between steps 18–24 to change surgical instruments.
Pause briefly (<30 sec) between steps 18–24 to check ligations or cannula placement.
Place the mouse on its back on a thermal-controlled surgical board.
Restrict the limbs gently using surgical tape to minimize movement during surgery.
Insert a rectal probe into the mouse for continuous body temperature monitoring at 37°C.
Make a lateral incision from the lower abdomen to the neck area carefully, avoiding puncturing the peritoneum.
Use blunt dissection to lift the skin away from the underlying peritoneal wall.
Make angled incisions pointing towards the limbs.
Gently pull back the skin.
Use blunt dissection to separate the skin from the underlying peritoneal wall.
Examine the tumor carefully, noting that it is vascularized by newly formed blood vessels originating from both cranial and caudal superficial epigastric artery and vein.
Remove the fascia connecting the skin to the peritoneal wall very carefully using the curved edge of the Dumont #7 forceps and surgical scissors if necessary.
Gently stretch the ends of the skin flap.
Immobilize the stretched skin flap by suturing.
Cut the ends of the suture.
Hold the suture in place with surgical tape.
Remove any non-vascularized fascia, connective or adipose tissue from the surface of the tumor to improve imaging quality.
Remove any residual fat from the tumor surface.
Gently lift and cut non-vascularized fascia or adipose tissue from the underlying tumor.
Apply hydrophobic ointment to the base of an appropriately sized stage insert.
Place the stage insert onto the microscope stage to generate a watertight seal.
Supperfuse the tumor with saline solution at 37°C.
Place a coverslip on top of the stage insert.
Cover the exposed tissue with a sterile cotton-gauze sheet.
Keep the tissue warm and perfused with saline at 37°C.
Apply a lubricating ophthalmic ointment to prevent drying of the animal’s eyes during imaging.
Remove or relax the temporary restraint on the limbs to allow for normal posture.
Scan the large exposed tumor to find a suitable region for imaging.
Inject vascular dyes, drugs, or cells while the tumor is being imaged to study real-time dynamics of immune cells in vivo.
Clean the microscope stage by wiping it down with 70% ethanol.
Use sterile surgical instruments for all steps.
Use sterile, surgical-grade cotton-gauze in this procedure.
Consider administration of analgesics during the surgical procedure as per institutional ethics protocols and experimental design.
Turn on the intravital microscope, including all laser components and detectors before starting mouse preparation.
Allow sufficient time for lasers and optics to warm up and stabilize.
Clean the microscope stage by wiping it down with 70% ethanol.
Transfer the imaging stage onto the microscope stage after surgical preparation of the tumor.
Scan the tissue using the eyepiece to locate the region of interest.
Determine an appropriate region of interest (ROI) based on endogenous fluorescence of transgenic immune cells or tumor cells.
Choose regions with blood vessels for studying leukocyte trafficking.
Ensure imaged regions reflect overall biology of the tissue and avoid biases due to selective imaging.
Switch the imaging to multiphoton mode.
Control imaging using computer-assisted software.
Euthanize the mice according to approved ethical guidelines after imaging is complete.
Save the imaging data.
Export the imaging data.
